This paper introduces the first comprehensive benchmark and toolkit for NSFW concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models. The reviewers reached a positive consensus (3x accept with either 3/5 or 4/5 confidence; 1 borderline accept with 3/5 confidence). The reviewer who rated the paper as a borderline accept was unresponsive through the rebuttal period, and so I have discounted their review compared to the other reviews. 

Overall, the reviewers cited the systematic evaluation of 13 methods, rigorous dataset construction, and practical guidance for real-world use. They also valued the inclusion of human (rather than AI-generated) ground-truth annotations, which were used to validate the automated NSFW classifiers. 

The main limitations of the paper were that (i) the dataset/benchmark only covers "three NSFW subcategories: nudity, violence, and horror" and (ii) all the experiments were conducted on Stable Diffusion v1.4 - which is largely considered an 'out-of-date' model. Towards (i), I and the other reviewers were satisfied with the authors' response that these three subcategories cover a substantial portion of unsafe content and are important to detect/erase in and of themselves. Towards (ii), the authors justified their choice of model on cost and reproducibility grounds, which I and the reviewers found reasonable. Despite these limitations, the paper's contributions remain broadly relevant and impactful. The ethics review also confirmed no issues. For the camera-ready, I recommend the authors (i) add more qualitative examples and failure cases, and (ii) include a discussion on applicability to newer models and broader unsafe content categories. 

I recommend acceptance as a poster as I believe this will serve as a valuable resource for communities working on content safety.

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for the thoughtful and constructive feedback that helped us improve our work. In address to the questions you raised, we have made responses below.

**L1**: Nudity, violence, and horror are representative NSFW themes that cover a substantial portion of unsafe content. Most baseline methods were evaluated only on nudity in their original papers(e.g., SalUn, SelfD, MACE), and even related benchmarks like UCANVAS and HUB do not assess as broad a range of NSFW themes as our study. We exclude hate and abuse content from evaluation because these themes are highly context-dependent and often lack distinctive visual signatures, making detection highly subjective and difficult to standardize without rich textual or contextual information.



**L2**: As lines 108–111, the human annotations were based on the category definitions provided in Appendix B. In most cases, annotators’ judgments are consistent. For the minority of cases where discrepancies arise (e.g., whether screaming indicates horror), we apply majority voting among annotators to minimize subjectivity, which is then formally quantified.

**L3**: We present the performance of SD 2.1 on NSFW content in Tab. 11 (App. G). To include it in core experiments and evaluate its behavior on specific themes, one would need to remove corresponding concept-related images from its original training data. However, as the native training dataset for SD 2.1 and Dalle is not publicly available, such experiments cannot be conducted. In real-world scenarios, cleaning training datasets also incurs high human effort. This motivates the development of concept erasure methods that solve this problem at a lower cost. These concept erasure methods are the primary focus of our evaluation.

**L4**: Both DALL·E 3 and Midjourney are closed-source models, which prevents us from accessing their code, let alone performing training. To tackle this, we carry out our experiments on a similar and open-source diffusion model—Stable Diffusion.

**L5**: For training, as lines 221–222, we follow the configurations and hyperparameters suggested in the original papers. For generating, each baseline diffuses 40 steps. To improve clarity, we have explicitly included method-specific settings and computational requirements as following table:

| **Methods** | **Lr** | **Steps** | **Other hyperparameters** |

| SD-NP | / | / | guidance scale=7.5 |

| ESD-u | 1e-5 | 1000 | start guidance=3; negative guidance=1 |

| AU | 1e-5 | 1000 | save interval=200; retain step=1; retain loss w=1; attack lr=1e-3; attack step=30; warmup iter=200; negative guidance=1 |
| AC | 2e-6 | 200 | / |
| SelfD | 1e-1 | 20 | lr scheduler=constant |
| SalUn | 1e-5 | 1000 | alpha=0.1; mask threshold=0.5; guidance scale=7.5 |
| MACE | 1e-5 | 50 | negative guidance=1.0; uncond loss weight=1 |


**L6**:  We initially reduced the display of unsafe images in the main paper out of consideration for reviewer comfort. However, we acknowledge that additional qualitative comparisons would help better illustrate differences across baselines. We have included more qualitative results in the revised version.

Thank you for the thoughtful and constructive feedback that helped us improve our work. In address to the questions you raised, we have made responses below.

**L1**: Baseline methods in the original papers were implemented using SD 1.4, due to its lower training cost. Besides, the choice of the base model does not inherently affect the effectiveness of the erasure methods themselves, as these base models are all based on the diffusion process and share similar modular designs. To ensure consistency across comparisons, we adopt a uniform backbone (SD 1.4) in all experiments.

**L2**: Nudity, violence, and horror are representative NSFW themes that cover a substantial portion of unsafe content. Most baseline methods were evaluated only on nudity in their original papers(e.g., SalUn, SelfD, MACE), and even related benchmarks like UCANVAS and HUB do not assess as broad a range of NSFW themes as our study. Compared to prior work, our benchmark represents a significant step forward in comprehensiveness. Self-harm, as mentioned, is grouped under violence in our benchmark due to strong visual similarities with violent content. We exclude hate and extremist content from evaluation because these themes are highly context-dependent and often lack distinctive visual signatures, making detection highly subjective and difficult to standardize without rich textual or contextual information.

**L3/Additional Feedback**: When selecting automated classifiers, we conducted human annotation as ground truth to identify those well-aligned with human judgments, ensuring reliable automatic evaluation in subsequent experiments. We initially reduced the display of unsafe images in the main paper out of consideration for reviewer comfort. However, we acknowledge that additional qualitative comparisons would help better illustrate differences across baselines. We have included more qualitative results in the revised version.

**L4**:  Thank you for pointing out the new related work. We have conducted additional experimental results on EraseDiff and Meta-Unlearning, which will be incorporated into the latest version. To the best of our knowledge, there is no existing TRACE-related work that directly intersects with our research area. The results are summarized below:

summary.value: This paper presents a comprehensive toolkit and evaluation benchmark for NSFW concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models. The authors develop a unified framework that covers dataset construction, a taxonomy of concept erasure methods, high-accuracy evaluation classifiers, and a suite of erasure effectiveness and generative quality metrics. Thirteen state-of-the-art NSFW concept erasure methods are systematically benchmarked under multiple scenarios, including erasure effectiveness, robustness to toxic prompts, sensitivity to data scale, and preservation of unrelated concepts. Extensive empirical results yield in-depth insights into the strengths and limitations of different approaches, and practical guidance is provided for real-world application. The code and toolkit are made publicly available to foster reproducibility and further research.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper addresses an important gap in the literature by offering the systematic and comprehensive evaluation of NSFW concept erasure methods specific to text-to-image diffusion models. The detailed comparison across 13 methods fills a major benchmarking void for practitioners and researchers.

2. The dataset construction process is rigorous, involving fine-grained thematic annotation for multiple NSFW themes across four publicly derived datasets, as shown in Figure 2. This enhances both the depth and breadth of the evaluation, making the benchmark valuable for multi-faceted content safety analyses.

3. The proposed taxonomy organizes concept erasure methods by data requirements and intervention stage, providing clear distinctions that help the community navigate the design space.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The authors propose four distinct Evaluation Perspectives: Erasure Effect to Target Concepts, Sensitivity to Training Data Scale, Robustness against Toxic Prompts, and Preservation of Irrelevant Concepts. However, I find the categorization of these perspectives somewhat problematic as they do not reside on the same logical level. For example, Erasure Effect to Target Concepts and Robustness against Toxic Prompts are both fundamentally assessing different facets of the core erasure effectiveness. In contrast, Preservation of Irrelevant Concepts measures an orthogonal aspect: the utility preservation or fidelity of the model concerning concepts unrelated to the erased NSFW content. 

2. A small concern is, well, the evaluation heavily relies on automated classifiers with human annotations as ground truth. Section 3.4 mentions varying tolerance levels and label ambiguities, but more analysis and discussion of classifier fairness, calibration, and cross-cultural/subjective differences in NSFW judgment would strengthen trust in the results. Are there cases where automated classifiers strongly disagree with human consensus, and how is this handled?

3. Although a variety of metrics are proposed (EP, GRD, FID, LPIPS, CLIPS, IR), most results are presented numerically. Limited qualitative visual analysis or ablation on how specific metric choices may drive conclusions is included.

4. A highly relevant and recent work is missing: ACE: Concept Editing in Diffusion Models without Performance Degradation.

5. Although Table 4 and Section 4.3 consider adversarial prompt robustness using RAB-generated prompts, concrete illustrations of real-world circumvention or failure scenarios are not deeply explored. But this is not a concern; rather, it is more like a suggestion.

summary.value: This work builds a comprehensive benchmark of concept erasure methods for diffusion models in text-to-image NSFW scenarios, which involves 13 concept erase methods and NSFW classifiers for evaluation. Moreover, the authors investigate the NSFW themes, data scales, and robustness to reveal the difference in the methods' capability.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This work provides a full-pipeline toolkit that allows practitioners can easily start their experiments.
2. They reveal the weak correlation between prompt toxicity and unsafe images, which emphasizes the importance of studying concept erasure techniques.
3. Beyond benchmarking existing concept removal methods for NSFW scenarios, the authors further evaluate the target themes, data scales, robustness, and the impact on the pre-trained diffusion model.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
While the authors reveal their benchmark results and analysis in detail, there are some unclear parts I would like to check.

1. Table 1 could be consistent with Section 4. For example, change the order of the column of **Taxonomy of Erasure Methods** and **Multi Themes**; group **Multi Themes** and **Data Scales** as the **Sensitivity to Training Data**.
2. In Sec 3.4, do you use fine-tuned NSFW-related classifiers for evaluating the discrepancies between human and model judgments? Because VQA could accurately capture different NSFW themes, could you provide which VQA model for image-text alignment scoring?
3. Following 2, in Lines 185-186, 'MHSC tends to be conservative, while VQA is more sensitive.' How do we get this conclusion? Do I miss something in the main manuscript?
4. In Lines 252-257 and Appendix H, could you provide the inference time besides comparing the training time? It is valuable to know that a concept earsure method's inference time when end-users use this diffusion model.
5. In Lines 247-248, 'This could be attributed to the fact that fine-tuning-based methods rely on concept-specific hyperparameters'. What are the *concept-specific hyperparameters*? Could you give an example? What are the sensitive hyperparameters that affect the benchmark results?
6. In Lines 273-276, '... fine-tuning-based methods perform poorly on the horror theme compared to other themes' and '... horror is a more abstract and context-dependent concept, often conveyed through mood, atmosphere, and symbolic imagery.' Could you explain the causation of context-dependent horror and the failure of poor performance of fine-tuning-based methods? What's the challenge of using a fine-tune-based method for horror-theme datasets?
7. In Line 288 ***Takeaways***, 'Blindly increasing the training data scale might offer limited benefits for most concept erasure methods'. How could we conclude it based on the previous paragraphs?

summary.value: The paper introduces the first end-to-end benchmark and toolkit for studying NSFW-concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models. It builds a pipeline that spans (i) five annotated datasets, (ii) a refined taxonomy covering 13 state-of-the-art erasure methods, (iii) automatic detectors, and (iv) metrics that jointly assess erasure success, image quality, semantic alignment and robustness. Extensive experiments on Stable-Diffusion-v1.4 compare post-hoc, parameter fine-tuning and data-cleaning approaches under four evaluation perspectives.

strengths_contributions.value:
- Prior work evaluates single methods or unsafe-image benchmarks (e.g. UnsafeD, HUB) but no comprehensive comparison exists for NSFW erasure; the paper fills this gap.
- Fine-grained annotations for nudity, violence, horror, enabling nuanced analysis.
- Extensive experiments – 13 SOTA baselines trained on SD-1.4 with open-sourced code; >80 k generations on A100 GPUs; training-time and hyperparam grids reported.
- Paper is easy to follow; tables/figures are informative 
- The insight provided for each experiments are quite interesting.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- I feel like it's asking too much but why all those entensive experiment are just based a single backbone :SD-v1.4. What's the rational of not using SD-XL or DALL·E 3? 
- NSFW themes is limited to nudity, violence, horror. However, hate, extremist, self-harm content are omitted. 
- One more thing is there is missing human evaluation. No user study on perceptual quality or residual NSFW; solely automated metrics may induce bias.
- Latest 2025 methods (EraseDiff, TRACE, Meta-Unlearning) absent from results.

ethical_considerations.value: Yes, there are ethics concerns that require attention by the authors

ethical_comments.value:
Safety and security
Benchmarked methods claim to remove NSFW content, but as the paper notes, adversarial prompts can circumvent many approaches. There's risk that tools may give false assurances of safety and be deployed where restricted content is undesirable (e.g., education, workplace).

Authors are encouraged to implement stronger threat models, including adaptive white-box attacks, and clearly report failure modes. They should also state caution for deployment contexts, recommending monitoring instead of blind trust.

dataset_code_comments.value: Code is well structured with clear datasets, evaluate, method. I trust the author on reproducibility.

additional_feedback.value: It would be great if author can try to address the limitation and ethical review. As for the easy fix for the human evaluation. I suggest author either provide a small cohort study to experiment 5.4. Or just add more example images.

final_justification.value: This work offers a timely, comparatively comprehensive benchmark for NSFW concept erasure in diffusion models, with open code and added experiments addressing key reviewer concerns. Given the scope, careful experimental design, and utility to the community, I would like to recommend acceptance.

summary.value: This paper presents a systematic benchmarking framework for evaluating concept erasure techniques aimed at removing not-safe-for-work (NSFW) content from text-to-image diffusion models.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper addresses a critical and underexplored problem in generative AI, which is the systematic evaluation of NSFW concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models. As public adoption of models like Stable Diffusion grows, so does the need for safety mechanisms. This work contributes a much-needed evaluation standard for developers and researchers seeking to deploy safer generative models (p.1-2).

2. The authors introduce the first comprehensive benchmark specifically tailored to NSFW concept erasure (Table 1, p.2), filling a notable gap left by existing works like UnsafeD [29], UCANVAS [45], and HUB [25], which either focus on base model safety or unrelated concepts such as style or object erasure.

3. The paper categorizes methods by the training stage, required data types, and targeted model components. The paper is clearly written and logically organized, with intuitive sectioning (e.g., Evaluation Framework, Results and Analysis), well-labeled tables (Table 1, Table 3, Table 4, Table 5), and informative figures (Figure 1: Evaluation pipeline; Figure 2: Dataset toxicity relationships).

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The benchmark focuses only on three NSFW subcategories: nudity, violence, and horror , explicitly excluding political, racial, or legally sensitive categories, which are common in real-world misuse cases (p.9, line 348). This narrow scope limits the benchmark’s coverage and generalization to broader definitions of “unsafe content.” I suggest that future versions could extend thematic coverage by incorporating additional categories such as hate speech, abuse, or misinformation, even if initially limited to small-scale annotations or partially automated detection.


2. While the paper performs fine-grained annotations via expert labeling (p.4, Sec. 3.2), it acknowledges inconsistencies in previous datasets ( I2P) and variability in human interpretation (p.6). However, no inter-annotator agreement metrics are reported, nor are steps taken to minimize subjectivity formally quantified.

3.Although dataset cleaning is listed as one category of erasure (Table 2), the paper excludes these methods from core experiments due to cost and impracticality (p.6, Sec. 4.1). However, this omits an important class of interventions used in commercial systems like DALLE 3 or SD2.1

4. All experiments are conducted using Stable Diffusion v1.4 as the base model (p.6, Sec. 4). This limits the generality of the findings to a single architecture and training dataset, while diffusion models like SD 2.1, DALLE 3, and Midjourney differ significantly in architecture, data curation, and filtering. My major concern is the results may not generalize to newer or commercial models with different inductive biases or pretrained safety filters.


5. Although the authors provide code (p.1), the main paper lacks clear documentation of certain implementation details such as training  time comparisons are deferred to Appendix H. Also, the hyperparameters, batch size and training epochs are not explained. A summary table of method-specific settings and computational requirements should be included in the main paper for transparency and reproducibility.


6.The paper does not include qualitative visual examples of failure cases, such as prompts that bypass erasure filters, unintended side effects. Without failure analysis, it's hard to understand where and why methods fail, especially in borderline or adversarial cases.

title.value: Comprehensive Assessment and Analysis for NSFW Content Erasure in Text-to-Image Diffusion models

abstract.value: Text-to-image diffusion models have gained widespread application across various domains, demonstrating remarkable creative potential. However, the strong generalization capabilities of diffusion models can inadvertently lead to the generation of not-safe-for-work (NSFW) content, posing significant risks to their safe deployment. While several concept erasure methods have been proposed to mitigate the issue associated with NSFW content, a comprehensive evaluation of their effectiveness across various scenarios remains absent. To bridge this gap, we introduce a full-pipeline toolkit specifically designed for concept erasure and conduct the first systematic study of NSFW concept erasure methods. By examining the interplay between the underlying mechanisms and empirical observations, we provide in-depth insights and practical guidance for the effective application of concept erasure methods in various real-world scenarios, with the aim of advancing the understanding of content safety in diffusion models and establishing a solid foundation for future research and development in this critical area.
